title: Demolition of collapsed structure at 25 West Mill Street
subtitle: Elora Greenspace building, adjacent owner's role, and Township legal and engineering costs paid from capital reserve
overview: At a special meeting, Council dealt with the stone structure at 25 West Mill Street, Elora, part of the Elora Greenspace. The Township leases the property from its owner, and the roof and part of the walls collapsed on February 24, 2025. Staff said the site was secured but needs prompt clean-up.

Council delegated authority to the Chief Administrative Officer to finalize and execute a temporary access and demolition agreement with the adjacent property owner, generally following the draft in the staff report {{vote:m1}}. The neighbouring owner's building is attached to the structure, and debris fell onto its land. Under the agreement, that owner arranges the demolition and has the best access for it.

Council also decided that the Township's own legal and consulting engineering costs will come from the general capital reserve rather than being reimbursed by the neighbouring owner. Councillors said this keeps public and private responsibilities and money separate. For residents, the aim is a quick, safe clean-up that protects the Greenspace, with no new by-law needed because authority was delegated to staff.

decisions.item: Demolition agreement for 25 West Mill Street
decisions.detail: Council delegated authority to the Chief Administrative Officer to finalize and execute a temporary access and demolition agreement, generally in accordance with the draft appended to Report CAO2025-03, for demolition and clean-up of the collapsed structure.

decisions.item: Funding of Township legal and engineering costs
decisions.detail: The Township's associated legal and consulting engineering costs will be funded from the general capital reserve instead of being reimbursed by the adjacent owner.

debate: One councillor supported the adjacent owner paying all demolition costs, but objected to that owner reimbursing the Township's legal and engineering costs. The concern was keeping public and private responsibility and money clearly divided, and avoiding any suggestion of influence.
Another councillor agreed the funding should be separated. A third said the Township should cover its own engineering and legal costs.

Staff noted the cost wording had to be changed in a second part of the resolution. Council then specified the Township's consulting engineer and legal costs, since some engineering work could relate to the neighbouring owner's attached building.

Asked who was responsible for the structure, staff said the Township was responsible under its lease. The building was not in use by the Township or anyone else, and staff did not believe it was being inspected.
Councillors commended the neighbouring owner for getting involved. One said the attached building looked concerning and that the extent of damage would only be known once work begins.
